[512](https://docs.rs#512)
[513](https://docs.rs#513)/// A **data structure** that can be deserialized from any data format supported
[514](https://docs.rs#514)/// by Serde.
[515](https://docs.rs#515)///
[516](https://docs.rs#516)/// Serde provides `Deserialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
[517](https://docs.rs#517)/// standard library types. The complete list is [here][crate::de]. All of these
[518](https://docs.rs#518)/// can be deserialized using Serde out of the box.
[519](https://docs.rs#519)///
[520](https://docs.rs#520)/// Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called `serde_derive` to
[521](https://docs.rs#521)/// automatically generate `Deserialize` implementations for structs and enums
[522](https://docs.rs#522)/// in your program. See the [derive section of the manual][derive] for how to
[523](https://docs.rs#523)/// use this.
[524](https://docs.rs#524)///
[525](https://docs.rs#525)/// In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Deserialize` manually for
[526](https://docs.rs#526)/// some type in your program. See the [Implementing
[527](https://docs.rs#527)/// `Deserialize`][impl-deserialize] section of the manual for more about this.
[528](https://docs.rs#528)///
[529](https://docs.rs#529)/// Third-party crates may provide `Deserialize` implementations for types that
[530](https://docs.rs#530)/// they expose. For example the `linked-hash-map` crate provides a
[531](https://docs.rs#531)/// `LinkedHashMap<K, V>` type that is deserializable by Serde because the crate
[532](https://docs.rs#532)/// provides an implementation of `Deserialize` for it.
[533](https://docs.rs#533)///
[534](https://docs.rs#534)/// [derive]: https://serde.rs/derive.html
[535](https://docs.rs#535)/// [impl-deserialize]: https://serde.rs/impl-deserialize.html
[536](https://docs.rs#536)///
[537](https://docs.rs#537)/// # Lifetime
[538](https://docs.rs#538)///
[539](https://docs.rs#539)/// The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
[540](https://docs.rs#540)/// borrowed by `Self` when deserialized. See the page [Understanding
[541](https://docs.rs#541)/// deserializer lifetimes] for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.
[542](https://docs.rs#542)///
[543](https://docs.rs#543)/// [Understanding deserializer lifetimes]: https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html
[544](https://docs.rs#544)#[cfg_attr(
[545](https://docs.rs#545)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[546](https://docs.rs#546)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[547](https://docs.rs#547)        // Prevents `serde_core::de::Deserialize` appearing in the error message
[548](https://docs.rs#548)        // in projects with no direct dependency on serde_core.
[549](https://docs.rs#549)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::Deserialize<'de>` is not satisfied",
[550](https://docs.rs#550)        note = "for local types consider adding `#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]` to your `{Self}` type",
[551](https://docs.rs#551)        note = "for types from other crates check whether the crate offers a `serde` feature flag",
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    )
[553](https://docs.rs#553))]
[554](https://docs.rs#554)pub trait [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/trait.Deserialize.html)<'de>: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
[555](https://docs.rs#555)    /// Deserialize this value from the given Serde deserializer.
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    ///
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    /// See the [Implementing `Deserialize`][impl-deserialize] section of the
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    /// manual for more information about how to implement this method.
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    ///
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    /// [impl-deserialize]: https://serde.rs/impl-deserialize.html
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, D::Error>
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    where
[563](https://docs.rs#563)        D: [Deserializer](https://docs.rs#945-1266)<'de>;
[564](https://docs.rs#564)
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    /// Deserializes a value into `self` from the given Deserializer.
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    ///
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    /// The purpose of this method is to allow the deserializer to reuse
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    /// resources and avoid copies. As such, if this method returns an error,
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    /// `self` will be in an indeterminate state where some parts of the struct
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    /// have been overwritten. Although whatever state that is will be
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    /// memory-safe.
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    ///
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    /// This is generally useful when repeatedly deserializing values that
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    /// are processed one at a time, where the value of `self` doesn't matter
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    /// when the next deserialization occurs.
[576](https://docs.rs#576)    ///
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    /// If you manually implement this, your recursive deserializations should
[578](https://docs.rs#578)    /// use `deserialize_in_place`.
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    ///
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    /// This method is stable and an official public API, but hidden from the
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    /// documentation because it is almost never what newbies are looking for.
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    /// Showing it in rustdoc would cause it to be featured more prominently
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    /// than it deserves.
[584](https://docs.rs#584)    #[doc(hidden)]
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    fn deserialize_in_place<D>(deserializer: D, place: &mut Self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<(), D::Error>
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    where
[587](https://docs.rs#587)        D: [Deserializer](https://docs.rs#945-1266)<'de>,
[588](https://docs.rs#588)    {
[589](https://docs.rs#589)        // Default implementation just delegates to `deserialize` impl.
[590](https://docs.rs#590)        *[place](https://docs.rs#585) = [tri!](https://docs.rs/lib.rs.html#111)(Deserialize::deserialize(deserializer));
[591](https://docs.rs#591)        [Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)(())
[592](https://docs.rs#592)    }
[593](https://docs.rs#593)}
[594](https://docs.rs#594)
[595](https://docs.rs#595)/// A data structure that can be deserialized without borrowing any data from
[596](https://docs.rs#596)/// the deserializer.
[597](https://docs.rs#597)///
[598](https://docs.rs#598)/// This is primarily useful for trait bounds on functions. For example a
[599](https://docs.rs#599)/// `from_str` function may be able to deserialize a data structure that borrows
[600](https://docs.rs#600)/// from the input string, but a `from_reader` function may only deserialize
[601](https://docs.rs#601)/// owned data.
[602](https://docs.rs#602)///
[603](https://docs.rs#603)/// ```edition2021
[604](https://docs.rs#604)/// # use serde::de::{Deserialize, DeserializeOwned};
[605](https://docs.rs#605)/// # use std::io::{Read, Result};
[606](https://docs.rs#606)/// #
[607](https://docs.rs#607)/// # trait Ignore {
[608](https://docs.rs#608)/// fn from_str<'a, T>(s: &'a str) -> Result<T>
[609](https://docs.rs#609)/// where
[610](https://docs.rs#610)///     T: Deserialize<'a>;
[611](https://docs.rs#611)///
[612](https://docs.rs#612)/// fn from_reader<R, T>(rdr: R) -> Result<T>
[613](https://docs.rs#613)/// where
[614](https://docs.rs#614)///     R: Read,
[615](https://docs.rs#615)///     T: DeserializeOwned;
[616](https://docs.rs#616)/// # }
[617](https://docs.rs#617)/// ```
[618](https://docs.rs#618)///
[619](https://docs.rs#619)/// # Lifetime
[620](https://docs.rs#620)///
[621](https://docs.rs#621)/// The relationship between `Deserialize` and `DeserializeOwned` in trait
[622](https://docs.rs#622)/// bounds is explained in more detail on the page [Understanding deserializer
[623](https://docs.rs#623)/// lifetimes].
[624](https://docs.rs#624)///
[625](https://docs.rs#625)/// [Understanding deserializer lifetimes]: https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html
[626](https://docs.rs#626)#[cfg_attr(
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[629](https://docs.rs#629)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::de::DeserializeOwned` is not satisfied",
[630](https://docs.rs#630)    )
[631](https://docs.rs#631))]
[632](https://docs.rs#632)pub trait [DeserializeOwned](https://docs.rs/serde_core/de/trait.DeserializeOwned.html): for<'de> [Deserialize](https://docs.rs#554-593)<'de> {}
[633](https://docs.rs#633)impl<T> [DeserializeOwned](https://docs.rs#632) for T where T: for<'de> [Deserialize](https://docs.rs#554-593)<'de> {}

[635](https://docs.rs#635)/// `DeserializeSeed` is the stateful form of the `Deserialize` trait. If you
[636](https://docs.rs#636)/// ever find yourself looking for a way to pass data into a `Deserialize` impl,
[637](https://docs.rs#637)/// this trait is the way to do it.
[638](https://docs.rs#638)///
[639](https://docs.rs#639)/// As one example of stateful deserialization consider deserializing a JSON
[640](https://docs.rs#640)/// array into an existing buffer. Using the `Deserialize` trait we could
[641](https://docs.rs#641)/// deserialize a JSON array into a `Vec<T>` but it would be a freshly allocated
[642](https://docs.rs#642)/// `Vec<T>`; there is no way for `Deserialize` to reuse a previously allocated
[643](https://docs.rs#643)/// buffer. Using `DeserializeSeed` instead makes this possible as in the
[644](https://docs.rs#644)/// example code below.
[645](https://docs.rs#645)///
[646](https://docs.rs#646)/// The canonical API for stateless deserialization looks like this:
[647](https://docs.rs#647)///
[648](https://docs.rs#648)/// ```edition2021
[649](https://docs.rs#649)/// # use serde::Deserialize;
[650](https://docs.rs#650)/// #
[651](https://docs.rs#651)/// # enum Error {}
[652](https://docs.rs#652)/// #
[653](https://docs.rs#653)/// fn func<'de, T: Deserialize<'de>>() -> Result<T, Error>
[654](https://docs.rs#654)/// # {
[655](https://docs.rs#655)/// #     unimplemented!()
[656](https://docs.rs#656)/// # }
[657](https://docs.rs#657)/// ```
[658](https://docs.rs#658)///
[659](https://docs.rs#659)/// Adjusting an API like this to support stateful deserialization is a matter
[660](https://docs.rs#660)/// of accepting a seed as input:
[661](https://docs.rs#661)///
[662](https://docs.rs#662)/// ```edition2021
[663](https://docs.rs#663)/// # use serde::de::DeserializeSeed;
[664](https://docs.rs#664)/// #
[665](https://docs.rs#665)/// # enum Error {}
[666](https://docs.rs#666)/// #
[667](https://docs.rs#667)/// fn func_seed<'de, T: DeserializeSeed<'de>>(seed: T) -> Result<T::Value, Error>
[668](https://docs.rs#668)/// # {
[669](https://docs.rs#669)/// #     let _ = seed;
[670](https://docs.rs#670)/// #     unimplemented!()
[671](https://docs.rs#671)/// # }
[672](https://docs.rs#672)/// ```
[673](https://docs.rs#673)///
[674](https://docs.rs#674)/// In practice the majority of deserialization is stateless. An API expecting a
[675](https://docs.rs#675)/// seed can be appeased by passing `std::marker::PhantomData` as a seed in the
[676](https://docs.rs#676)/// case of stateless deserialization.
[677](https://docs.rs#677)///
[678](https://docs.rs#678)/// # Lifetime
[679](https://docs.rs#679)///
[680](https://docs.rs#680)/// The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
[681](https://docs.rs#681)/// borrowed by `Self::Value` when deserialized. See the page [Understanding
[682](https://docs.rs#682)/// deserializer lifetimes] for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.
[683](https://docs.rs#683)///
[684](https://docs.rs#684)/// [Understanding deserializer lifetimes]: https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html
[685](https://docs.rs#685)///
[686](https://docs.rs#686)/// # Example
[687](https://docs.rs#687)///
[688](https://docs.rs#688)/// Suppose we have JSON that looks like `[[1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6]]` and we need
[689](https://docs.rs#689)/// to deserialize it into a flat representation like `vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`.
[690](https://docs.rs#690)/// Allocating a brand new `Vec<T>` for each subarray would be slow. Instead we
[691](https://docs.rs#691)/// would like to allocate a single `Vec<T>` and then deserialize each subarray
[692](https://docs.rs#692)/// into it. This requires stateful deserialization using the `DeserializeSeed`
[693](https://docs.rs#693)/// trait.
[694](https://docs.rs#694)///
[695](https://docs.rs#695)/// ```edition2021
[696](https://docs.rs#696)/// use serde::de::{Deserialize, DeserializeSeed, Deserializer, SeqAccess, Visitor};
[697](https://docs.rs#697)/// use std::fmt;
[698](https://docs.rs#698)/// use std::marker::PhantomData;
[699](https://docs.rs#699)///
[700](https://docs.rs#700)/// // A DeserializeSeed implementation that uses stateful deserialization to
[701](https://docs.rs#701)/// // append array elements onto the end of an existing vector. The preexisting
[702](https://docs.rs#702)/// // state ("seed") in this case is the Vec<T>. The `deserialize` method of
[703](https://docs.rs#703)/// // `ExtendVec` will be traversing the inner arrays of the JSON input and
[704](https://docs.rs#704)/// // appending each integer into the existing Vec.
[705](https://docs.rs#705)/// struct ExtendVec<'a, T: 'a>(&'a mut Vec<T>);
[706](https://docs.rs#706)///
[707](https://docs.rs#707)/// impl<'de, 'a, T> DeserializeSeed<'de> for ExtendVec<'a, T>
[708](https://docs.rs#708)/// where
[709](https://docs.rs#709)///     T: Deserialize<'de>,
[710](https://docs.rs#710)/// {
[711](https://docs.rs#711)///     // The return type of the `deserialize` method. This implementation
[712](https://docs.rs#712)///     // appends onto an existing vector but does not create any new data
[713](https://docs.rs#713)///     // structure, so the return type is ().
[714](https://docs.rs#714)///     type Value = ();
[715](https://docs.rs#715)///
[716](https://docs.rs#716)///     fn deserialize<D>(self, deserializer: D) -> Result<Self::Value, D::Error>
[717](https://docs.rs#717)///     where
[718](https://docs.rs#718)///         D: Deserializer<'de>,
[719](https://docs.rs#719)///     {
[720](https://docs.rs#720)///         // Visitor implementation that will walk an inner array of the JSON
[721](https://docs.rs#721)///         // input.
[722](https://docs.rs#722)///         struct ExtendVecVisitor<'a, T: 'a>(&'a mut Vec<T>);
[723](https://docs.rs#723)///
[724](https://docs.rs#724)///         impl<'de, 'a, T> Visitor<'de> for ExtendVecVisitor<'a, T>
[725](https://docs.rs#725)///         where
[726](https://docs.rs#726)///             T: Deserialize<'de>,
[727](https://docs.rs#727)///         {
[728](https://docs.rs#728)///             type Value = ();
[729](https://docs.rs#729)///
[730](https://docs.rs#730)///             fn expecting(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[731](https://docs.rs#731)///                 write!(formatter, "an array of integers")
[732](https://docs.rs#732)///             }
[733](https://docs.rs#733)///
[734](https://docs.rs#734)///             fn visit_seq<A>(self, mut seq: A) -> Result<(), A::Error>
[735](https://docs.rs#735)///             where
[736](https://docs.rs#736)///                 A: SeqAccess<'de>,
[737](https://docs.rs#737)///             {
[738](https://docs.rs#738)///                 // Decrease the number of reallocations if there are many elements
[739](https://docs.rs#739)///                 if let Some(size_hint) = seq.size_hint() {
[740](https://docs.rs#740)///                     self.0.reserve(size_hint);
[741](https://docs.rs#741)///                 }
[742](https://docs.rs#742)///
[743](https://docs.rs#743)///                 // Visit each element in the inner array and push it onto
[744](https://docs.rs#744)///                 // the existing vector.
[745](https://docs.rs#745)///                 while let Some(elem) = seq.next_element()? {
[746](https://docs.rs#746)///                     self.0.push(elem);
[747](https://docs.rs#747)///                 }
[748](https://docs.rs#748)///                 Ok(())
[749](https://docs.rs#749)///             }
[750](https://docs.rs#750)///         }
[751](https://docs.rs#751)///
[752](https://docs.rs#752)///         deserializer.deserialize_seq(ExtendVecVisitor(self.0))
[753](https://docs.rs#753)///     }
[754](https://docs.rs#754)/// }
[755](https://docs.rs#755)///
[756](https://docs.rs#756)/// // Visitor implementation that will walk the outer array of the JSON input.
[757](https://docs.rs#757)/// struct FlattenedVecVisitor<T>(PhantomData<T>);
[758](https://docs.rs#758)///
[759](https://docs.rs#759)/// impl<'de, T> Visitor<'de> for FlattenedVecVisitor<T>
[760](https://docs.rs#760)/// where
[761](https://docs.rs#761)///     T: Deserialize<'de>,
[762](https://docs.rs#762)/// {
[763](https://docs.rs#763)///     // This Visitor constructs a single Vec<T> to hold the flattened
[764](https://docs.rs#764)///     // contents of the inner arrays.
[765](https://docs.rs#765)///     type Value = Vec<T>;
[766](https://docs.rs#766)///
[767](https://docs.rs#767)///     fn expecting(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[768](https://docs.rs#768)///         write!(formatter, "an array of arrays")
[769](https://docs.rs#769)///     }
[770](https://docs.rs#770)///
[771](https://docs.rs#771)///     fn visit_seq<A>(self, mut seq: A) -> Result<Vec<T>, A::Error>
[772](https://docs.rs#772)///     where
[773](https://docs.rs#773)///         A: SeqAccess<'de>,
[774](https://docs.rs#774)///     {
[775](https://docs.rs#775)///         // Create a single Vec to hold the flattened contents.
[776](https://docs.rs#776)///         let mut vec = Vec::new();
[777](https://docs.rs#777)///
[778](https://docs.rs#778)///         // Each iteration through this loop is one inner array.
[779](https://docs.rs#779)///         while let Some(()) = seq.next_element_seed(ExtendVec(&mut vec))? {
[780](https://docs.rs#780)///             // Nothing to do; inner array has been appended into `vec`.
[781](https://docs.rs#781)///         }
[782](https://docs.rs#782)///
[783](https://docs.rs#783)///         // Return the finished vec.
[784](https://docs.rs#784)///         Ok(vec)
[785](https://docs.rs#785)///     }
[786](https://docs.rs#786)/// }
[787](https://docs.rs#787)///
[788](https://docs.rs#788)/// # fn example<'de, D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<(), D::Error>
[789](https://docs.rs#789)/// # where
[790](https://docs.rs#790)/// #     D: Deserializer<'de>,
[791](https://docs.rs#791)/// # {
[792](https://docs.rs#792)/// let visitor = FlattenedVecVisitor(PhantomData);
[793](https://docs.rs#793)/// let flattened: Vec<u64> = deserializer.deserialize_seq(visitor)?;
[794](https://docs.rs#794)/// #     Ok(())
[795](https://docs.rs#795)/// # }
[796](https://docs.rs#796)/// ```
[797](https://docs.rs#797)#[cfg_attr(
[798](https://docs.rs#798)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[799](https://docs.rs#799)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[800](https://docs.rs#800)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::de::DeserializeSeed<'de>` is not satisfied",
[801](https://docs.rs#801)    )
[802](https://docs.rs#802))]

[806](https://docs.rs#806)

[830](https://docs.rs#830)
[831](https://docs.rs#831)/// A **data format** that can deserialize any data structure supported by
[832](https://docs.rs#832)/// Serde.
[833](https://docs.rs#833)///
[834](https://docs.rs#834)/// The role of this trait is to define the deserialization half of the [Serde
[835](https://docs.rs#835)/// data model], which is a way to categorize every Rust data type into one of
[836](https://docs.rs#836)/// 29 possible types. Each method of the `Deserializer` trait corresponds to one
[837](https://docs.rs#837)/// of the types of the data model.
[838](https://docs.rs#838)///
[839](https://docs.rs#839)/// Implementations of `Deserialize` map themselves into this data model by
[840](https://docs.rs#840)/// passing to the `Deserializer` a `Visitor` implementation that can receive
[841](https://docs.rs#841)/// these various types.
[842](https://docs.rs#842)///
[843](https://docs.rs#843)/// The types that make up the Serde data model are:
[844](https://docs.rs#844)///
[845](https://docs.rs#845)///  - **14 primitive types**
[846](https://docs.rs#846)///    - bool
[847](https://docs.rs#847)///    - i8, i16, i32, i64, i128
[848](https://docs.rs#848)///    - u8, u16, u32, u64, u128
[849](https://docs.rs#849)///    - f32, f64
[850](https://docs.rs#850)///    - char
[851](https://docs.rs#851)///  - **string**
[852](https://docs.rs#852)///    - UTF-8 bytes with a length and no null terminator.
[853](https://docs.rs#853)///    - When serializing, all strings are handled equally. When deserializing,
[854](https://docs.rs#854)///      there are three flavors of strings: transient, owned, and borrowed.
[855](https://docs.rs#855)///  - **byte array** - \[u8\]
[856](https://docs.rs#856)///    - Similar to strings, during deserialization byte arrays can be
[857](https://docs.rs#857)///      transient, owned, or borrowed.
[858](https://docs.rs#858)///  - **option**
[859](https://docs.rs#859)///    - Either none or some value.
[860](https://docs.rs#860)///  - **unit**
[861](https://docs.rs#861)///    - The type of `()` in Rust. It represents an anonymous value containing
[862](https://docs.rs#862)///      no data.
[863](https://docs.rs#863)///  - **unit_struct**
[864](https://docs.rs#864)///    - For example `struct Unit` or `PhantomData<T>`. It represents a named
[865](https://docs.rs#865)///      value containing no data.
[866](https://docs.rs#866)///  - **unit_variant**
[867](https://docs.rs#867)///    - For example the `E::A` and `E::B` in `enum E { A, B }`.
[868](https://docs.rs#868)///  - **newtype_struct**
[869](https://docs.rs#869)///    - For example `struct Millimeters(u8)`.
[870](https://docs.rs#870)///  - **newtype_variant**
[871](https://docs.rs#871)///    - For example the `E::N` in `enum E { N(u8) }`.
[872](https://docs.rs#872)///  - **seq**
[873](https://docs.rs#873)///    - A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example `Vec<T>`
[874](https://docs.rs#874)///      or `HashSet<T>`. When serializing, the length may or may not be known
[875](https://docs.rs#875)///      before iterating through all the data. When deserializing, the length
[876](https://docs.rs#876)///      is determined by looking at the serialized data.
[877](https://docs.rs#877)///  - **tuple**
[878](https://docs.rs#878)///    - A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
[879](https://docs.rs#879)///      length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
[880](https://docs.rs#880)///      serialized data, for example `(u8,)` or `(String, u64, Vec<T>)` or
[881](https://docs.rs#881)///      `[u64; 10]`.
[882](https://docs.rs#882)///  - **tuple_struct**
[883](https://docs.rs#883)///    - A named tuple, for example `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`.
[884](https://docs.rs#884)///  - **tuple_variant**
[885](https://docs.rs#885)///    - For example the `E::T` in `enum E { T(u8, u8) }`.
[886](https://docs.rs#886)///  - **map**
[887](https://docs.rs#887)///    - A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example `BTreeMap<K, V>`.
[888](https://docs.rs#888)///  - **struct**
[889](https://docs.rs#889)///    - A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
[890](https://docs.rs#890)///      will be known at deserialization time without looking at the serialized
[891](https://docs.rs#891)///      data, for example `struct S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.
[892](https://docs.rs#892)///  - **struct_variant**
[893](https://docs.rs#893)///    - For example the `E::S` in `enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`.
[894](https://docs.rs#894)///
[895](https://docs.rs#895)/// The `Deserializer` trait supports two entry point styles which enables
[896](https://docs.rs#896)/// different kinds of deserialization.
[897](https://docs.rs#897)///
[898](https://docs.rs#898)/// 1. The `deserialize_any` method. Self-describing data formats like JSON are
[899](https://docs.rs#899)///    able to look at the serialized data and tell what it represents. For
[900](https://docs.rs#900)///    example the JSON deserializer may see an opening curly brace (`{`) and
[901](https://docs.rs#901)///    know that it is seeing a map. If the data format supports
[902](https://docs.rs#902)///    `Deserializer::deserialize_any`, it will drive the Visitor using whatever
[903](https://docs.rs#903)///    type it sees in the input. JSON uses this approach when deserializing
[904](https://docs.rs#904)///    `serde_json::Value` which is an enum that can represent any JSON
[905](https://docs.rs#905)///    document. Without knowing what is in a JSON document, we can deserialize
[906](https://docs.rs#906)///    it to `serde_json::Value` by going through
[907](https://docs.rs#907)///    `Deserializer::deserialize_any`.
[908](https://docs.rs#908)///
[909](https://docs.rs#909)/// 2. The various `deserialize_*` methods. Non-self-describing formats like
[910](https://docs.rs#910)///    Postcard need to be told what is in the input in order to deserialize it.
[911](https://docs.rs#911)///    The `deserialize_*` methods are hints to the deserializer for how to
[912](https://docs.rs#912)///    interpret the next piece of input. Non-self-describing formats are not
[913](https://docs.rs#913)///    able to deserialize something like `serde_json::Value` which relies on
[914](https://docs.rs#914)///    `Deserializer::deserialize_any`.
[915](https://docs.rs#915)///
[916](https://docs.rs#916)/// When implementing `Deserialize`, you should avoid relying on
[917](https://docs.rs#917)/// `Deserializer::deserialize_any` unless you need to be told by the
[918](https://docs.rs#918)/// Deserializer what type is in the input. Know that relying on
[919](https://docs.rs#919)/// `Deserializer::deserialize_any` means your data type will be able to
[920](https://docs.rs#920)/// deserialize from self-describing formats only, ruling out Postcard and many
[921](https://docs.rs#921)/// others.
[922](https://docs.rs#922)///
[923](https://docs.rs#923)/// [Serde data model]: https://serde.rs/data-model.html
[924](https://docs.rs#924)///
[925](https://docs.rs#925)/// # Lifetime
[926](https://docs.rs#926)///
[927](https://docs.rs#927)/// The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
[928](https://docs.rs#928)/// borrowed from the input when deserializing. See the page [Understanding
[929](https://docs.rs#929)/// deserializer lifetimes] for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.
[930](https://docs.rs#930)///
[931](https://docs.rs#931)/// [Understanding deserializer lifetimes]: https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html
[932](https://docs.rs#932)///
[933](https://docs.rs#933)/// # Example implementation
[934](https://docs.rs#934)///
[935](https://docs.rs#935)/// The [example data format] presented on the website contains example code for
[936](https://docs.rs#936)/// a basic JSON `Deserializer`.
[937](https://docs.rs#937)///
[938](https://docs.rs#938)/// [example data format]: https://serde.rs/data-format.html
[939](https://docs.rs#939)#[cfg_attr(
[940](https://docs.rs#940)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[941](https://docs.rs#941)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[942](https://docs.rs#942)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::de::Deserializer<'de>` is not satisfied",
[943](https://docs.rs#943)    )
[944](https://docs.rs#944))]

[1186](https://docs.rs#1186)    /// Determine whether `Deserialize` implementations should expect to
[1187](https://docs.rs#1187)    /// deserialize their human-readable form.
[1188](https://docs.rs#1188)    ///
[1189](https://docs.rs#1189)    /// Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to
[1190](https://docs.rs#1190)    /// construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient.
[1191](https://docs.rs#1191)    /// Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the
[1192](https://docs.rs#1192)    /// human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the
[1193](https://docs.rs#1193)    /// compact one.
[1194](https://docs.rs#1194)    ///
[1195](https://docs.rs#1195)    /// ```edition2021
[1196](https://docs.rs#1196)    /// # use std::ops::Add;
[1197](https://docs.rs#1197)    /// # use std::str::FromStr;
[1198](https://docs.rs#1198)    /// #
[1199](https://docs.rs#1199)    /// # struct Timestamp;
[1200](https://docs.rs#1200)    /// #
[1201](https://docs.rs#1201)    /// # impl Timestamp {
[1202](https://docs.rs#1202)    /// #     const EPOCH: Timestamp = Timestamp;
[1203](https://docs.rs#1203)    /// # }
[1204](https://docs.rs#1204)    /// #
[1205](https://docs.rs#1205)    /// # impl FromStr for Timestamp {
[1206](https://docs.rs#1206)    /// #     type Err = String;
[1207](https://docs.rs#1207)    /// #     fn from_str(_: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Err> {
[1208](https://docs.rs#1208)    /// #         unimplemented!()
[1209](https://docs.rs#1209)    /// #     }
[1210](https://docs.rs#1210)    /// # }
[1211](https://docs.rs#1211)    /// #
[1212](https://docs.rs#1212)    /// # struct Duration;
[1213](https://docs.rs#1213)    /// #
[1214](https://docs.rs#1214)    /// # impl Duration {
[1215](https://docs.rs#1215)    /// #     fn seconds(_: u64) -> Self { unimplemented!() }
[1216](https://docs.rs#1216)    /// # }
[1217](https://docs.rs#1217)    /// #
[1218](https://docs.rs#1218)    /// # impl Add<Duration> for Timestamp {
[1219](https://docs.rs#1219)    /// #     type Output = Timestamp;
[1220](https://docs.rs#1220)    /// #     fn add(self, _: Duration) -> Self::Output {
[1221](https://docs.rs#1221)    /// #         unimplemented!()
[1222](https://docs.rs#1222)    /// #     }
[1223](https://docs.rs#1223)    /// # }
[1224](https://docs.rs#1224)    /// #
[1225](https://docs.rs#1225)    /// use serde::de::{self, Deserialize, Deserializer};
[1226](https://docs.rs#1226)    ///
[1227](https://docs.rs#1227)    /// impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for Timestamp {
[1228](https://docs.rs#1228)    ///     fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error>
[1229](https://docs.rs#1229)    ///     where
[1230](https://docs.rs#1230)    ///         D: Deserializer<'de>,
[1231](https://docs.rs#1231)    ///     {
[1232](https://docs.rs#1232)    ///         if deserializer.is_human_readable() {
[1233](https://docs.rs#1233)    ///             // Deserialize from a human-readable string like "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
[1234](https://docs.rs#1234)    ///             let s = String::deserialize(deserializer)?;
[1235](https://docs.rs#1235)    ///             Timestamp::from_str(&s).map_err(de::Error::custom)
[1236](https://docs.rs#1236)    ///         } else {
[1237](https://docs.rs#1237)    ///             // Deserialize from a compact binary representation, seconds since
[1238](https://docs.rs#1238)    ///             // the Unix epoch.
[1239](https://docs.rs#1239)    ///             let n = u64::deserialize(deserializer)?;
[1240](https://docs.rs#1240)    ///             Ok(Timestamp::EPOCH + Duration::seconds(n))
[1241](https://docs.rs#1241)    ///         }
[1242](https://docs.rs#1242)    ///     }
[1243](https://docs.rs#1243)    /// }
[1244](https://docs.rs#1244)    /// ```
[1245](https://docs.rs#1245)    ///
[1246](https://docs.rs#1246)    /// The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
[1247](https://docs.rs#1247)    /// may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
[1248](https://docs.rs#1248)    /// support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
[1249](https://docs.rs#1249)    /// human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
[1250](https://docs.rs#1250)    /// change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
[1251](https://docs.rs#1251)    /// deserialize from the same data in compact mode.
[1252](https://docs.rs#1252)    #[inline]
[1253](https://docs.rs#1253)    fn is_human_readable(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html) {
[1254](https://docs.rs#1254)        true
[1255](https://docs.rs#1255)    }
[1256](https://docs.rs#1256)
[1257](https://docs.rs#1257)    // Not public API.
[1258](https://docs.rs#1258)    #[cfg(all(not(no_serde_derive), any(feature = "std", feature = "alloc")))]
[1259](https://docs.rs#1259)    #[doc(hidden)]
[1260](https://docs.rs#1260)    fn __deserialize_content_v1<V>(self, visitor: V) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<V::Value, Self::Error>
[1261](https://docs.rs#1261)    where
[1262](https://docs.rs#1262)        V: [Visitor](https://docs.rs#1317-1720)<'de, Value = crate::private::[Content](https://docs.rs/private/content.rs.html#10-39)<'de>>,
[1263](https://docs.rs#1263)    {
[1264](https://docs.rs#1264)        [self](https://docs.rs#1260).[deserialize_any](https://docs.rs#959-961)([visitor](https://docs.rs#1260))
[1265](https://docs.rs#1265)    }

[1270](https://docs.rs#1270)/// This trait represents a visitor that walks through a deserializer.
[1271](https://docs.rs#1271)///
[1272](https://docs.rs#1272)/// # Lifetime
[1273](https://docs.rs#1273)///
[1274](https://docs.rs#1274)/// The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the requirement for lifetime of data
[1275](https://docs.rs#1275)/// that may be borrowed by `Self::Value`. See the page [Understanding
[1276](https://docs.rs#1276)/// deserializer lifetimes] for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.
[1277](https://docs.rs#1277)///
[1278](https://docs.rs#1278)/// [Understanding deserializer lifetimes]: https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html
[1279](https://docs.rs#1279)///
[1280](https://docs.rs#1280)/// # Example
[1281](https://docs.rs#1281)///
[1282](https://docs.rs#1282)/// ```edition2021
[1283](https://docs.rs#1283)/// # use serde::de::{self, Unexpected, Visitor};
[1284](https://docs.rs#1284)/// # use std::fmt;
[1285](https://docs.rs#1285)/// #
[1286](https://docs.rs#1286)/// /// A visitor that deserializes a long string - a string containing at least
[1287](https://docs.rs#1287)/// /// some minimum number of bytes.
[1288](https://docs.rs#1288)/// struct LongString {
[1289](https://docs.rs#1289)///     min: usize,
[1290](https://docs.rs#1290)/// }
[1291](https://docs.rs#1291)///
[1292](https://docs.rs#1292)/// impl<'de> Visitor<'de> for LongString {
[1293](https://docs.rs#1293)///     type Value = String;
[1294](https://docs.rs#1294)///
[1295](https://docs.rs#1295)///     fn expecting(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[1296](https://docs.rs#1296)///         write!(formatter, "a string containing at least {} bytes", self.min)
[1297](https://docs.rs#1297)///     }
[1298](https://docs.rs#1298)///
[1299](https://docs.rs#1299)///     fn visit_str<E>(self, s: &str) -> Result<Self::Value, E>
[1300](https://docs.rs#1300)///     where
[1301](https://docs.rs#1301)///         E: de::Error,
[1302](https://docs.rs#1302)///     {
[1303](https://docs.rs#1303)///         if s.len() >= self.min {
[1304](https://docs.rs#1304)///             Ok(s.to_owned())
[1305](https://docs.rs#1305)///         } else {
[1306](https://docs.rs#1306)///             Err(de::Error::invalid_value(Unexpected::Str(s), &self))
[1307](https://docs.rs#1307)///         }
[1308](https://docs.rs#1308)///     }
[1309](https://docs.rs#1309)/// }
[1310](https://docs.rs#1310)/// ```
[1311](https://docs.rs#1311)#[cfg_attr(
[1312](https://docs.rs#1312)    not(no_diagnostic_namespace),
[1313](https://docs.rs#1313)    diagnostic::on_unimplemented(
[1314](https://docs.rs#1314)        message = "the trait bound `{Self}: serde::de::Visitor<'de>` is not satisfied",
[1315](https://docs.rs#1315)    )
[1316](https://docs.rs#1316))]

# IntoDeserializer in serde_core::de - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.IntoDeserializer.html

`pub trait IntoDeserializer<'de, E: `[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Error.html) = [Error](https://docs.rs/value/struct.Error.html)> {
    type [Deserializer](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Deserializer): [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)<'de, Error = E>;
    // Required method
    fn [into_deserializer](https://docs.rs#tymethod.into_deserializer)(self) -> Self::[Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoDeserializer.html#associatedtype.Deserializer);
}## Expand description

Converts an existing value into a `Deserializer` from which other values can
be deserialized.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
borrowed from the resulting `Deserializer`. See the page [Understanding
deserializer lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html) for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::de::{value, Deserialize, IntoDeserializer};
use serde_derive::Deserialize;
use std::str::FromStr;
#[derive(Deserialize)]
enum Setting {
    On,
    Off,
}
impl FromStr for Setting {
    type Err = value::Error;
    fn from_str(s: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Err> {
        Self::deserialize(s.into_deserializer())
    }
}
```

# Expected in serde_core::de - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Expected.html

## Expand description

`Expected` represents an explanation of what data a `Visitor` was expecting
to receive.

This is used as an argument to the `invalid_type`, `invalid_value`, and
`invalid_length` methods of the `Error` trait to build error messages. The
message should be a noun or noun phrase that completes the sentence “This
Visitor expects to receive …”, for example the message could be “an
integer between 0 and 64”. The message should not be capitalized and should
not end with a period.

Within the context of a `Visitor` implementation, the `Visitor` itself
(`&self`) is an implementation of this trait.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn visit_bool<E>(self, v: bool) -> Result<Self::Value, E>
where
    E: de::Error,
{
    Err(de::Error::invalid_type(Unexpected::Bool(v), &self))
}
```
Outside of a `Visitor`, `&"..."` can be used.

# Serialize in serde_core::ser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html

```
pub trait Serialize {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[serialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize)<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<S::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), S::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where S: [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html);
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be serialized into any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Serialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/index.html). All of
these can be serialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [ serde_derive](https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive) to
automatically generate

`Serialize` implementations for structs and enums in
your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html)for how to use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Serialize` manually for some
type in your program. See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the
manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Serialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the [ linked-hash-map](https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map) crate provides a

[type that is serializable by Serde because the crate provides an implementation of](https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html)

`LinkedHashMap<K, V>``Serialize` for it.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize this value into the given Serde serializer.

See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the manual for more
information about how to implement this method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
// This is what #[derive(Serialize)] would generate.
impl Serialize for Person {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut s = serializer.serialize_struct("Person", 3)?;
        s.serialize_field("name", &self.name)?;
        s.serialize_field("age", &self.age)?;
        s.serialize_field("phones", &self.phones)?;
        s.end()
    }
}
```

# Deserialize in serde_core::de - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html

`pub trait Deserialize<'de>: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [deserialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.deserialize)<D>(deserializer: D) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, D::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where D: [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)<'de>;
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be deserialized from any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Deserialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/index.html). All of these
can be deserialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called `serde_derive` to
automatically generate `Deserialize` implementations for structs and enums
in your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html) for how to
use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Deserialize` manually for
some type in your program. See the [Implementing
 Deserialize](https://serde.rs/impl-deserialize.html) section of the manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Deserialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the `linked-hash-map` crate provides a
`LinkedHashMap<K, V>` type that is deserializable by Serde because the crate
provides an implementation of `Deserialize` for it.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
borrowed by `Self` when deserialized. See the page [Understanding
deserializer lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html) for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.

### impl<'de, T> [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)<'de> for [Rc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/rc/struct.Rc.html)<T>

**crate feature**only.

`rc` and (crate features `std` or `alloc`)Deserializing a data structure containing `Rc` will not attempt to
deduplicate `Rc` references to the same data. Every deserialized `Rc`
will end up with a strong count of 1.

[is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

A **data format** that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

The role of this trait is to define the serialization half of the [Serde
data model](https://serde.rs/data-model.html), which is a way to categorize every Rust data structure into one
of 29 possible types. Each method of the `Serializer` trait corresponds to
one of the types of the data model.

Implementations of `Serialize` map themselves into this data model by
invoking exactly one of the `Serializer` methods.

The types that make up the Serde data model are:

- **14 primitive types**- bool
- i8, i16, i32, i64, i128
- u8, u16, u32, u64, u128
- f32, f64
- char

- **string**- UTF-8 bytes with a length and no null terminator.
- When serializing, all strings are handled equally. When deserializing, there are three flavors of strings: transient, owned, and borrowed.

- **byte array**- [u8]- Similar to strings, during deserialization byte arrays can be transient, owned, or borrowed.

- **option**- Either none or some value.

- **unit**- The type of `()`in Rust. It represents an anonymous value containing no data.

- The type of
- **unit_struct**- For example `struct Unit`or`PhantomData<T>`. It represents a named value containing no data.

- For example
- **unit_variant**- For example the `E::A`and`E::B`in`enum E { A, B }`.

- For example the
- **newtype_struct**- For example `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

- For example
- **newtype_variant**- For example the `E::N`in`enum E { N(u8) }`.

- For example the
- **seq**- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
`Vec<T>`or`HashSet<T>`. When serializing, the length may or may not be known before iterating through all the data. When deserializing, the length is determined by looking at the serialized data.

- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
- **tuple**- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `(u8,)`or`(String, u64, Vec<T>)`or`[u64; 10]`.

- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **tuple_struct**- A named tuple, for example `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`.

- A named tuple, for example
- **tuple_variant**- For example the `E::T`in`enum E { T(u8, u8) }`.

- For example the
- **map**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example `BTreeMap<K, V>`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example
- **struct**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `struct S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **struct_variant**- For example the `E::S`in`enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`.

- For example the

Many Serde serializers produce text or binary data as output, for example
JSON or Postcard. This is not a requirement of the `Serializer` trait, and
there are serializers that do not produce text or binary output. One example
is the `serde_json::value::Serializer` (distinct from the main `serde_json`
serializer) that produces a `serde_json::Value` data structure in memory as
output.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-implementation)Example implementation

The [example data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html) presented on the website contains example code for
a basic JSON `Serializer`.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

The output type produced by this `Serializer` during successful
serialization. Most serializers that produce text or binary output
should set `Ok = ()` and serialize into an [ io::Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html) or buffer
contained within the

`Serializer` instance. Serializers that build
in-memory data structures may be simplified by using `Ok` to propagate
the data structure around.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize an `i8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i8` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i16` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i32` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize a `u8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u8` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u16` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u32` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize an `f32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `f32` and `f64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `f64` and
forward to `serialize_f64`.

Serialize a character.

If the format does not support characters, it is reasonable to serialize
it as a single element `str` or a `u32`.

Serialize a chunk of raw byte data.

Enables serializers to serialize byte slices more compactly or more
efficiently than other types of slices. If no efficient implementation
is available, a reasonable implementation would be to forward to
`serialize_seq`. If forwarded, the implementation looks usually just
like this:

Serialize a unit struct like `struct Unit` or `PhantomData<T>`.

A reasonable implementation would be to forward to `serialize_unit`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Nothing;
impl Serialize for Nothing {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.serialize_unit_struct("Nothing")
    }
}
```

Serialize a unit variant like `E::A` in `enum E { A, B }`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, and the `variant` is the name of the
variant.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
enum E {
    A,
    B,
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::A => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 0, "A"),
            E::B => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 1, "B"),
        }
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#916-922)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#916-922)

Serialize a newtype struct like `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

Serializers are encouraged to treat newtype structs as insignificant
wrappers around the data they contain. A reasonable implementation would
be to forward to `value.serialize(self)`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Millimeters(u8);
impl Serialize for Millimeters {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.serialize_newtype_struct("Millimeters", &self.0)
    }
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#950-958)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#950-958)

Serialize a newtype variant like `E::N` in `enum E { N(u8) }`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, and the `variant` is the name of the
variant. The `value` is the data contained within this newtype variant.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
enum E {
    M(String),
    N(u8),
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::M(ref s) => serializer.serialize_newtype_variant("E", 0, "M", s),
            E::N(n) => serializer.serialize_newtype_variant("E", 1, "N", &n),
        }
    }
}
```

#### fn [serialize_seq](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_seq)(
    self,
    len: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.usize.html)>,

Begin to serialize a variably sized sequence. This call must be
followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`, then a call to
`end`.

The argument is the number of elements in the sequence, which may or may not be computable before the sequence is iterated. Some serializers only support sequences whose length is known up front.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeSeq, Serializer};
impl<T> Serialize for Vec<T>
where
    T: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut seq = serializer.serialize_seq(Some(self.len()))?;
        for element in self {
            seq.serialize_element(element)?;
        }
        seq.end()
    }
}
```

Begin to serialize a statically sized sequence whose length will be
known at deserialization time without looking at the serialized data.
This call must be followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`,
then a call to `end`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTuple, Serializer};
impl<A, B, C> Serialize for (A, B, C)
where
    A: Serialize,
    B: Serialize,
    C: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut tup = serializer.serialize_tuple(3)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.0)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.1)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.2)?;
        tup.end()
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTuple, Serializer};
const VRAM_SIZE: usize = 386;
struct Vram([u16; VRAM_SIZE]);
impl Serialize for Vram {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut seq = serializer.serialize_tuple(VRAM_SIZE)?;
        for element in &self.0[..] {
            seq.serialize_element(element)?;
        }
        seq.end()
    }
}
```

                tv.serialize_field(a)?;

                tv.serialize_field(c)?;

Begin to serialize a map. This call must be followed by zero or more
calls to `serialize_key` and `serialize_value`, then a call to `end`.

The argument is the number of elements in the map, which may or may not be computable before the map is iterated. Some serializers only support maps whose length is known up front.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeMap, Serializer};
impl<K, V> Serialize for HashMap<K, V>
where
    K: Serialize,
    V: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut map = serializer.serialize_map(Some(self.len()))?;
        for (k, v) in self {
            map.serialize_entry(k, v)?;
        }
        map.end()
    }
}
```

    S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 },
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::S {
                ref r,
                ref g,
                ref b,
            } => {
                let mut sv = serializer.serialize_struct_variant("E", 0, "S", 3)?;
                sv.serialize_field("r", r)?;
                sv.serialize_field("g", g)?;
                sv.serialize_field("b", b)?;
                sv.end()
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Collect an iterator as a sequence.

The default implementation serializes each item yielded by the iterator
using [ serialize_seq](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize_seq). Implementors should not need to override this
method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct SecretlyOneHigher {
    data: Vec<i32>,
}
impl Serialize for SecretlyOneHigher {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_seq(self.data.iter().map(|x| x + 1))
    }
}

use std::collections::BTreeSet;
struct MapToUnit {
    keys: BTreeSet<i32>,
}
// Serializes as a map in which the values are all unit.
impl Serialize for MapToUnit {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_map(self.keys.iter().map(|k| (k, ())))
    }
}

use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
impl Serialize for DateTime {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_str(&format_args!("{:?}{:?}", self.naive_local(), self.offset()))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#1459-1461)#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#1459-1461)

#### fn [is_human_readable](https://docs.rs#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.bool.html)

Determine whether `Serialize` implementations should serialize in
human-readable form.

Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient. Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the compact one.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
impl Serialize for Timestamp {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        if serializer.is_human_readable() {
            // Serialize to a human-readable string "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
            self.to_string().serialize(serializer)
        } else {
            // Serialize to a compact binary representation.
            self.seconds_since_epoch().serialize(serializer)
        }
    }
}
```
The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
deserialize from the same data in compact mode.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

    StartRequest,

impl Display for MessageType {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        self.serialize(f)
    }
}

# DeserializeOwned in serde_core::de - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.DeserializeOwned.html

`pub trait DeserializeOwned: for<'de> `[Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)<'de> { }## Expand description

A data structure that can be deserialized without borrowing any data from the deserializer.

This is primarily useful for trait bounds on functions. For example a
`from_str` function may be able to deserialize a data structure that borrows
from the input string, but a `from_reader` function may only deserialize
owned data.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn from_str<'a, T>(s: &'a str) -> Result<T>
where
    T: Deserialize<'a>;
fn from_reader<R, T>(rdr: R) -> Result<T>
where
    R: Read,
    T: DeserializeOwned;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

The relationship between `Deserialize` and `DeserializeOwned` in trait
bounds is explained in more detail on the page [Understanding deserializer
lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html).

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# winit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fission-winit/0.30.13-fission.1/winit/

## Expand description

Winit is a cross-platform window creation and event loop management library.

[§](https://docs.rs#building-windows)Building windows

Before you can create a [ Window](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html), you first need to build an

[. This is done with the](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.EventLoop.html)

`EventLoop`[function.](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.EventLoop.html#method.new)

`EventLoop::new()````
use winit::event_loop::EventLoop;
fn main() {
    let event_loop = EventLoop::new().unwrap();
    // ...
}
```
Then you create a [ Window](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html) with

[.](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.ActiveEventLoop.html#method.create_window)

`create_window`[§](https://docs.rs#event-handling)Event handling

Once a [ Window](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html) has been created, it will generate different

*events*. A

[object can generate](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html)

`Window`[s when certain input events occur, such as a cursor moving over the window or a key getting pressed while the window is focused. Devices can generate](https://docs.rs/event/enum.WindowEvent.html)

`WindowEvent`[s, which contain unfiltered event data that isn’t specific to a certain window. Some user activity, like mouse movement, can generate both a](https://docs.rs/event/enum.DeviceEvent.html)

`DeviceEvent`

`WindowEvent`*and*a

[. You can also create and handle your own custom](https://docs.rs/event/enum.DeviceEvent.html)

`DeviceEvent`[s, if desired.](https://docs.rs/event/enum.Event.html#variant.UserEvent)

`Event::UserEvent`You can retrieve events by calling [ EventLoop::run_app()](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.EventLoop.html#method.run_app). This function will
dispatch events for every

[that was created with that particular](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html)

`Window`[, and will run until](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.EventLoop.html)

`EventLoop`[is used, at which point](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.ActiveEventLoop.html#method.exit)

`exit()`[.](https://docs.rs/event/enum.Event.html#variant.LoopExiting)

`Event::LoopExiting`Winit no longer uses a `EventLoop::poll_events() -> impl Iterator<Event>`-based event loop
model, since that can’t be implemented properly on some platforms (e.g web, iOS) and works
poorly on most other platforms. However, this model can be re-implemented to an extent with
`EventLoopExtPumpEvents::pump_app_events()` 1. See that method’s documentation for more reasons about why
it’s discouraged beyond compatibility reasons.

```
use winit::application::ApplicationHandler;
use winit::event::WindowEvent;
use winit::event_loop::{ActiveEventLoop, ControlFlow, EventLoop};
use winit::window::{Window, WindowId};
#[derive(Default)]
struct App {
    window: Option<Window>,
}
impl ApplicationHandler for App {
    fn resumed(&mut self, event_loop: &ActiveEventLoop) {
        self.window = Some(event_loop.create_window(Window::default_attributes()).unwrap());
    }
    fn window_event(&mut self, event_loop: &ActiveEventLoop, id: WindowId, event: WindowEvent) {
        match event {
            WindowEvent::CloseRequested => {
                println!("The close button was pressed; stopping");
                event_loop.exit();
            },
            WindowEvent::RedrawRequested => {
                // Redraw the application.
                //
                // It's preferable for applications that do not render continuously to render in
                // this event rather than in AboutToWait, since rendering in here allows
                // the program to gracefully handle redraws requested by the OS.
                // Draw.
                // Queue a RedrawRequested event.
                //
                // You only need to call this if you've determined that you need to redraw in
                // applications which do not always need to. Applications that redraw continuously
                // can render here instead.
                self.window.as_ref().unwrap().request_redraw();
            }
            _ => (),
        }
    }
}
fn main() {
    let event_loop = EventLoop::new().unwrap();
    // ControlFlow::Poll continuously runs the event loop, even if the OS hasn't
    // dispatched any events. This is ideal for games and similar applications.
    event_loop.set_control_flow(ControlFlow::Poll);
    // ControlFlow::Wait pauses the event loop if no events are available to process.
    // This is ideal for non-game applications that only update in response to user
    // input, and uses significantly less power/CPU time than ControlFlow::Poll.
    event_loop.set_control_flow(ControlFlow::Wait);
    let mut app = App::default();
    event_loop.run_app(&mut app);
}
```
[ WindowEvent](https://docs.rs/event/enum.WindowEvent.html) has a

[member. In multi-window environments, it should be compared to the value returned by](https://docs.rs/window/struct.WindowId.html)

`WindowId`[to determine which](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html#method.id)

`Window::id()`[dispatched the event.](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html)

`Window`[§](https://docs.rs#drawing-on-the-window)Drawing on the window

Winit doesn’t directly provide any methods for drawing on a [ Window](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html). However, it allows you
to retrieve the raw handle of the window and display (see the

[module and/or the](https://docs.rs/platform/index.html)

`platform`[and](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html#method.raw_window_handle)

`raw_window_handle`[methods), which in turn allows you to create an OpenGL/Vulkan/DirectX/Metal/etc. context that can be used to render graphics.](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html#method.raw_display_handle)

`raw_display_handle`Note that many platforms will display garbage data in the window’s client area if the
application doesn’t render anything to the window by the time the desktop compositor is ready to
display the window to the user. If you notice this happening, you should create the window with
[ visible set to false](https://docs.rs/window/struct.WindowAttributes.html#method.with_visible) and explicitly make
the window visible only once you’re ready to render into it.

[§](https://docs.rs#ui-scaling)UI scaling

UI scaling is important, go read the docs for the [ dpi](https://docs.rs/dpi/index.html) crate for an
introduction.

All of Winit’s functions return physical types, but can take either logical or physical coordinates as input, allowing you to use the most convenient coordinate system for your particular application.

Winit will dispatch a [ ScaleFactorChanged](https://docs.rs/event/enum.WindowEvent.html#variant.ScaleFactorChanged) event whenever a window’s scale factor has changed.
This can happen if the user drags their window from a standard-resolution monitor to a high-DPI
monitor or if the user changes their DPI settings. This allows you to rescale your application’s
UI elements and adjust how the platform changes the window’s size to reflect the new scale
factor. If a window hasn’t received a

[event, its scale factor can be found by calling](https://docs.rs/event/enum.WindowEvent.html#variant.ScaleFactorChanged)

`ScaleFactorChanged`[.](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html#method.scale_factor)

`window.scale_factor()`[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

Winit provides the following Cargo features:

- `x11`(enabled by default): On Unix platforms, enables the X11 backend.
- `wayland`(enabled by default): On Unix platforms, enables the Wayland backend.
- `rwh_04`: Implement- `raw-window-handle v0.4`traits.
- `rwh_05`: Implement- `raw-window-handle v0.5`traits.
- `rwh_06`: Implement- `raw-window-handle v0.6`traits.
- `serde`: Enables serialization/deserialization of certain types with- [Serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde).
- `mint`: Enables mint (math interoperability standard types) conversions.

See the [ platform](https://docs.rs/platform/index.html) module for documentation on platform-specific cargo
features.

# hanzo-kernel 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.0

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.0/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

hanzo-kernel: Hanzo's first-party GPU kernel DSL.

Write a kernel ONCE in Rust; it lowers to CUDA / ROCm / Vulkan / Metal. This crate is the
first-party facade over the CubeCL lowering engine: kernel source names only `hanzo_kernel::*`,
never `cubecl`. "Values, not places" -- CubeCL is the implementation value; `hanzo_kernel` is the
stable namespace we build against, so the engine can be upgraded (or forked) without touching a
single kernel.

The perf primitives our hand-tuned kernels rely on are all here and lower to the native instruction on each backend:

- `dot`on a vectorized- `Line<i8>`-> dp4a / OpSDotAccSat (int8 4-way dot)
- `cmma`-> tensor cores (WMMA / cooperative-matrix / simdgroup)
- `SharedMemory`,- `plane_*`(subgroup reduce/shuffle),- `Atomic`, barriers

MIGRATION POLICY (perf-gated, never a downgrade): the DSL provides COVERAGE -- every quant type on every backend, from one source, killing the "same op, N impls, N numeric behaviors" bug class. A hand-tuned kernel is replaced by its DSL twin ONLY when the DSL version is bit-exact AND within perf noise (bench-gated). Where a hand-tuned kernel still wins, it stays as the specialized peak path and the DSL is the portable fallback for the backends that lack a tuned version.

# hdf5_metno - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hdf5-metno/0.13.0/hdf5_metno/

## Expand description

HDF5 for Rust.

This crate provides thread-safe Rust bindings and high-level wrappers for the `HDF5`
library API. Some of the features include:

- Thread-safety with non-threadsafe libhdf5 builds guaranteed via reentrant mutexes.
- Native representation of most HDF5 types, including variable-length strings and arrays.
- Derive-macro for automatic mapping of user structs and enums to `HDF5`types.
- Multi-dimensional array reading/writing interface via `ndarray`.

Direct low-level bindings are also available and provided in the `hdf5-sys` crate.

Requires `HDF5` library of version 1.8.4 or later. Newer versions will enable additional
features of the library. Such items are marked in the documentation with a version number
indicating the required version of `HDF5`. The `have-direct` and `have-parallel` features
also indicates `HDF5` functionality.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# swarm_abm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/swarm-abm/0.3.0/swarm_abm/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#swarm-abm)swarm-abm

Spatial agent-based modeling (ABM) engine: agents on a 2D grid, configurable scheduling, time-series data collection, and deterministic reproducibility (same seed → same results).

[§](https://docs.rs#concepts)Concepts

- `Agent`
- `Model`
- `Grid2D`
- `Schedule`- `decide`with an immutable model +- `apply`).
- `DataCollector`
- `Simulation`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-random-walkers)Example: random walkers

```
use swarm_abm::prelude::*;
struct Walker {
    pos: Pos,
}
struct World {
    agents: AgentSet<Walker>,
    visits: Grid2D<u32>,
}
impl Agent for Walker {
    type Model = World;
    fn step(&mut self, _id: AgentId, world: &mut World, rng: &mut SimRng) {
        if let Some(dest) =
            world.visits.random_neighbor(self.pos, Neighborhood::Moore, rng)
        {
            self.pos = dest;
            world.visits[self.pos] += 1;
        }
    }
}
impl Model for World {
    type Agent = Walker;
    fn agents(&self) -> &AgentSet<Walker> {
        &self.agents
    }
    fn agents_mut(&mut self) -> &mut AgentSet<Walker> {
        &mut self.agents
    }
}
let mut agents = AgentSet::new();
agents.insert(Walker { pos: Pos::new(5, 5) });
let visits = Grid2D::new(10, 10).with_torus(true);
let mut sim = Simulation::new(World { agents, visits }, 42);
sim.add_reporter("total_visits", |w: &World| {
    w.visits.iter().map(|(_, &v)| f64::from(v)).sum()
});
sim.run(100);
assert_eq!(sim.step_count(), 100);
assert_eq!(sim.data().series("total_visits").unwrap().last(), Some(&100.0));
```

- [data](https://docs.rs/data/index.html)

# capsudod-pwauth 0.1.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capsudod-pwauth/0.1.2

# capsudo-rs

`sudo`, but [object-capability style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object-capability_model) — a Rust reimplementation of
[capsudo](https://github.com/kaniini/capsudo) built so the capability channel
can be **proxied across  Edera Protect zones over IDM**, not just a
local Unix socket.

## The idea

Privilege is not granted by a setuid bit. A privileged daemon (`capsudod`) is
started ahead of time, already holding the privilege you want to delegate, and
bound to a *transport endpoint*. Whoever can reach that endpoint can invoke the
capability. The endpoint **is** the capability.

In the original, the endpoint is always an `AF_UNIX` socket whose file
permissions decide who may connect. Here the transport is abstracted: the same
protocol and the same client/daemon logic run unchanged over a local Unix
socket *or* a cross-zone IDM channel, so a capability held in one Edera zone can
be exposed to another without either side knowing the difference.

## What this enables

The motivating deployment is autonomous AI agents. An agent is sandboxed precisely because what it runs cannot be fully trusted, yet real work needs a few privileged operations: push this image, run that deploy script, restart a wedged service. The conventional escapes all grant ambient, stealable authority. A kubeconfig or SSH key mounted into the sandbox works from anywhere once exfiltrated, and sudo inside the sandbox puts privilege in the one place most likely to be prompt-injected.

capsudo restates the problem in object-capability terms. The agent's zone
holds no credentials at all; it holds an endpoint, and reaching the endpoint
is the permission. The daemon side fixes the command and environment (`-f`,
`-E`), so even a fully compromised client can only cause the pre-approved
operation to run. There is nothing to steal: the endpoint does not exist
outside the zone it was granted to, and its effect cannot be broadened from
the client side.

For the caller nothing changes: prefix a command, keep ordinary
stdin/stdout/stderr, exit codes, and fully interactive ptys, whether the
daemon is local or in another zone. In an Edera Protect deployment the grants
are declarative: the zone agent launches and manages the attenuated `capsudod`
instances from configuration and proxies an endpoint like `/run/cap/<name>`
into each authorized zone over IDM.

## Why a rewrite was needed for cross-zone

Two things in the original assume a shared kernel:

-
**Descriptor passing.**The caller's stdin/stdout/stderr are handed to the daemon over`SCM_RIGHTS`. File descriptors are meaningless across a zone boundary. Here the transport layer papers over that — real`SCM_RIGHTS`locally,**simulated**descriptor passing (stream multiplexing + local pipe ends) cross-zone — transparently, so client and daemon never learn which happened.
-
**The interactive pty.**The original allocates the pty on the*client*and ships the slave. A pty slave is a real terminal; a socket pair (all a cross-zone link can fabricate) is not. So the pty is allocated on the**daemon**side instead: the child always gets a genuine controlling terminal in its own zone, and only a byte stream plus window-size updates cross the channel. (The C version was updated to match.)

## Workspace layout

| Crate | Role |
|---|---|
| `capsudo-proto` | Transport-agnostic wire protocol: message types, portable fixed-endianness framing. No I/O. |
| `capsudo-transport` | `Transport`/`Listener`traits + implementations:`unix`(real`SCM_RIGHTS`),`mux`(simulated fd-passing over any byte channel),`fakeidm`(throwaway TCP cross-zone stub, feature`fakeidm`). |
| `capsudo-core` | Client and daemon session logic, written entirely against the traits. |
| `capsudo` | Client binary. |
| `capsudod` | Daemon binary (listening, or one-shot on stdin). |
| `capsudod-pwauth` | Authenticating front-end: shadow-password check, then chain to `capsudod`. Local sockets only: it identifies the caller via`SO_PEERCRED`, which does not exist across zones. |

## Build & test

```
cargo build
cargo test
cargo build --features capsudo-transport/fakeidm    # include the fake IDM stub
```
## Command-line

```
# Delegate "run anything" to whoever can reach the socket:
capsudod -S /run/capsudo/sudo -o root:wheel -m 0770 &
capsudo  -S /run/capsudo/sudo -- id
# Pin an exact command (client args ignored):
capsudod -S /run/capsudo/reboot -f /sbin/reboot &
capsudo  -S /run/capsudo/reboot
# Require a password first, then chain to capsudod:
capsudod-pwauth -S /run/capsudo/auth -o root:wheel -m 0770 -- capsudod &
capsudo -S /run/capsudo/auth -- id
```
See `CLAUDE.md` for the architecture in depth.

# capsudo_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capsudo-core/0.1.2/capsudo_core/

## Expand description

Client and daemon session logic for capsudo, generic over any
[ Transport](https://docs.rs/capsudo-transport/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capsudo_transport/traits/trait.Transport.html).

This crate contains the actual capsudo behaviour — the configuration handshake, attenuation policy, and program execution — with no knowledge of whether it is talking over a local Unix socket or a cross-zone IDM channel.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.ClientRequest.html)- Request
- What the client is asking the daemon to do.
- [Daemon](https://docs.rs/struct.DaemonConfig.html)- Config
- Daemon-side policy applied to every session.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Core](https://docs.rs/enum.CoreError.html)- Error
- Errors arising from the client or daemon session logic.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/enum.SessionOutcome.html)- Outcome
- How a client session ended.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_winsize.html)- winsize
- Reads the current terminal dimensions from `fd`.
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_client.html)- client
- Runs a client session to completion and returns the target program’s exit
status. Treats an authentication challenge as an error; use `run_session`
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_session.html)- session
- Runs one client session, optionally presenting `secret`for authentication.
- [serve_](https://docs.rs/fn.serve_connection.html)- connection
- Serves a single client connection: receives configuration, runs the program, and reports the exit status.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- Convenience result alias for core operations.
